x: Commentary on Sūrat [Has there come upon the human being]
n
. In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘Has there come upon the human being a span of time when he was not a thing mentioned? (1) We created the human being from a mixed drop to test him, and made him hearing and seeing
n

.’ Abū Jaʿfar says: By ‘Has there come upon the human being,’ God means that a time did indeed come upon him. Here ‘has’ introduces an affirmation, not a denial—like asking someone, ‘Have I not honored you?’ when one has honored him, or ‘Have I not visited you?’ when one has. Elsewhere it can be a denial, as in ‘Would anyone do such a thing?’ meaning that no one would. The human being meant here is Adam, peace be upon him. Qatādah likewise said that it is Adam: a span of time passed over him when he was not yet a thing mentioned, for humanity was only recently created and no creature of God is known to have been created after humankind. Qatādah said Adam, the Prophet, was the last of creation whom God created. Sufyān likewise identified the human being in the verse as Adam.
The interpreters differed about the length of the ‘span of time’ mentioned here.

Some said it was forty years: Adam’s clay remained fashioned in human form without the spirit being breathed into it for forty years. Thus a period passed over him while he was a formed body, a thing but not yet a thing mentioned; they said ‘not a thing mentioned’ means he had no distinction, rank, or honor, being only clinging clay and altered mud.

Others said no fixed length is intended. It is not naturally understood to say that a span of time passed over a person before he existed and before he was a thing; if that were meant, it would say that a time passed before he was created. The ‘time’ itself has no limit specified here.

His saying, ‘We created the human being from a mixed drop to test him’: God means that We created Adam’s descendants from a drop, that is, from the man’s fluid and the woman’s fluid. A nuṭfah is any small amount of liquid in a container, whether a well, waterskin, or something else. As ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥah said in a verse, ‘You are nothing but a drop in a worn waterskin.’ ‘Mixed’ means blended; its singular is mashj or mashīj, comparable to khidn and khadīn. Ruʾbah ibn al-ʿAjjāj said: ‘They cast every premature, squalling one, not yet clothed in skin, amid mixed blood.’ One says ‘I mixed this with that’; it is mixed with it. Abū Dhuʾayb likewise said of feathers and an arrow’s nock that they were blended together.
The interpreters differed about the mixture intended here.

Some said it is the mixing of the man’s fluid with the woman’s. Among those who held this view: ʿIkrimah said the man’s fluid and the woman’s fluid are mixed together. He also described them as blending. Ibn ʿAbbās said the woman’s fluid and the man’s fluid are mixed. Al-Suddī transmitted a similar explanation from Ibn ʿAbbās, and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said that when the two fluids come together they are mixed. Al-Ḥasan likewise said the woman’s fluid is blended with the man’s. Mujāhid said God creates a child from the man’s fluid and the woman’s fluid, as God says, ‘We created you from a male and a female’ (Q 49:13). He also said the child is created from successive portions of the two fluids.

Others said the verse means that the human being is created from a drop that passes through different forms: first a drop, then a clot, then a lump, then bones, which are then covered with flesh. Ibn ʿAbbās described the stages as originating from dust, then the fluid of the womb, then a drop, clot, lump, bones, and flesh, after which the person is brought forth as a new creation. ʿIkrimah listed the stages as drop, clot, lump, and bones. ʿIkrimah likewise said: a drop, then a clot. Qatādah explained ‘a mixed drop’ as the stages of creation: first a drop, then a clot, a lump, and bones; God then clothed the bones with flesh and brought the person forth as another creation, causing hair to grow. He also said ‘mixed’ means the blending of fluid and blood, after which it became a clot and then a lump.

Others said it refers to the differing colors of the drop. Ibn ʿAbbās said its colors are varied, and Mujāhid also described it as having different colors. Mujāhid said that whichever of the two fluids comes first determines whether the child resembles the paternal or maternal uncles. He also said the fluids have different colors: the man’s is white and red, while the woman’s is red and green.

Others said ‘mixed’ refers to the veins in the drop. ʿAbd Allāh said it means its veins; another report says these are the veins that occur in the drop. Al-Ṭabarī considers the soundest view to be that it means the man’s fluid mixed with the woman’s, since God calls it a mixed drop. Once it changes into a clot, it is no longer a drop, so it would not be apt to call the clot a mixed drop. As for the claim that the man’s fluid is white and red, what is commonly known is that it is one color, white tending toward red, not a mixture of colors. He supposes those who said ‘veins’ intended this meaning. Ibn ʿAbbās said the human is created from only a small quantity of fluid: one can see something like a tiny thread in a child after it is miscarried, and the son of Adam is created from something like that small amount of the mixed drop. His saying, ‘to test him’ means to try him. Some Arab grammarians said the meaning is ‘We made him hearing and seeing in order to test him,’ with the purpose stated first and the creation then explained.

Al-Ṭabarī says that interpretation is not sound: the test is possible through sound faculties and an uninjured intellect, even if hearing and sight are absent. Rather, God’s mention of granting us hearing and sight reminds us of His blessings and points us to our duty of gratitude. The test is being created with a sound natural disposition and an intellect free of impairment, as God says, ‘I created jinn and humankind only that they may worship Me’ (Q 51:56).

His saying, ‘We made him hearing and seeing’: We gave him hearing with which to hear and sight with which to see, as a favor and mercy to His servants and as proof against them. ‘I created jinn and humankind only that they may worship Me’ (Q 51:56).
His saying, ‘and made him hearing and seeing’: God made him able to hear and able to see, granting this blessing to His servants out of mercy and establishing an argument against them.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘We guided him to the way, whether he is grateful or ungrateful (3). We have prepared for the disbelievers chains, shackles, and a blazing Fire (4).’ God means: We have made the way to Paradise clear to the human being and shown him its path, whether he gives thanks or disbelieves. On this interpretation, ‘whether … or’ expresses the alternative outcome. It may also have the same sense as in ‘Either He will punish them or turn to them in mercy’ (Q 9:106), with ‘grateful or ungrateful’ describing the person guided: We guided him to the way, whether wretched or blessed. A grammarian of Basra gave this interpretation, comparing it with ‘either the punishment or the Hour’ (Q 19:75). The phrase can also be begun anew with the following word in the nominative.
The interpreters gave similar explanations.

Mujāhid explained ‘We guided him to the way’ as referring to wretchedness and felicity. Qatādah said ‘grateful’ means grateful for the blessings and ‘ungrateful’ means ungrateful for them. Ibn Zayd said God tests what a person will do, which of the two paths he will take and which of the two courses he will choose.

His saying, ‘We have prepared for the disbelievers chains’: God has prepared chains for those who reject His blessings and disobey His command, so that they may be firmly bound in Hell. ‘And shackles’ means that their hands will be fastened to their necks with shackles there.
His saying, ‘and a blazing Fire’: a fire kindled for them until it is aflame.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘The righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is camphor (5), a spring from which God’s servants drink, making it gush forth abundantly (6).’ God means those who were righteous in obeying their Lord, fulfilling His obligations, and avoiding disobedience. They will drink from a cup, meaning any vessel containing a drink. Its mixture—what is blended into its drink—is camphor, that is, camphor-like in its pleasant fragrance. It is also said that Camphor is the name of a spring in Paradise. Those who take that view construe ‘a spring’ as an apposition explaining Camphor; those who take Camphor as a description of the drink construe ‘a spring’ differently. On the latter interpretation, ‘a spring’ is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier, with ‘camphor’ as the predicate of ‘was.’ A third possibility is that it is governed by ‘drink’: the righteous drink from a spring, from a cup whose mixture is camphor. It could also be accusative as praise. Most interpreters, however, said camphor describes the drink. Mujāhid said it is mixed with camphor. Qatādah said a people will have it mixed with camphor and sealed for them with musk.

His saying, ‘a spring from which God’s servants drink’: the mixture in the cup from which these righteous people drink is like camphor in its pleasant fragrance; it comes from a spring from which God’s servants, whom He admits to Paradise, drink. On this interpretation, ‘a spring’ is a circumstantial qualifier related to the pronoun in ‘its mixture.’ ‘They drink by it’ means they are refreshed and benefit from it; it is also said that ‘drink by it’ and ‘drink it’ have the same meaning. Al-Farrāʾ mentioned that someone recited a verse in support of this usage. ‘They drank from the sea’s water, then rose up—how many green waves, with a roaring sound!’ By ‘how many’ in this verse the poet means ‘from’; similarly, one may say both ‘he speaks with good speech’ and ‘he speaks good speech.’

His saying, ‘making it gush forth abundantly’: they cause that spring from which they drink to flow wherever and however they wish in their dwellings and palaces. ‘Making it gush’ means causing it to pour and run.

The interpreters said similarly. Mujāhid said they direct it wherever they wish; in another report he said they lead it wherever they wish. Qatādah said its water is entirely at their disposal and they make it flow wherever they wish. Sufyān said of ‘making it gush forth abundantly’ that they direct it wherever they wish.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘They fulfill their vows and fear a Day whose evil will be widespread (7), and they give food, despite their love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive (8), saying: “We feed you only for God’s sake; we desire from you neither recompense nor thanks” (9).’ God means that the righteous who drink from the cup whose mixture is camphor were righteous by fulfilling the vows they made to God in obedience to Him. Mujāhid said they fulfill vows made in regard to God’s due. Qatādah said they vowed acts of obedience, including prayer, almsgiving, pilgrimage, and lesser pilgrimage, as well as what had been made obligatory upon them; God therefore called them righteous. Qatādah also explained the Day’s evil as spreading until it fills the heavens and earth, and said a person should not fulfill a vow to sever kinship, withhold charity, or do something evil, nor should he expiate it by keeping such a vow.

Qatādah explained fulfilling vows as obedience to God, prayer, pilgrimage, and lesser pilgrimage. Sufyān said the vows are fulfilled so long as they do not involve disobedience. The sentence omits an understood phrase: ‘the righteous … were fulfilling their vows’; ‘were’ is omitted because the context indicates it. A vow is anything a person obligates himself to do. ʿAntarah said: ‘They insulted my honor, though I did not insult theirs; and the two who vowed my blood, should I meet them …’ ‘They fear a Day whose evil will be widespread’ means they fear God’s punishment if they fail to fulfill their vows to do good. Its evil will be far-reaching, long-lasting, and pervasive. Qatādah said the evil of that Day will spread until it fills the heavens and earth. A person should not vow to cut off family ties, refrain from charity, or do wrong, and should not fulfill such a vow. One says that a crack spreads through glass when it extends and widens; the word is not used of a wall in this way.
Al-Aʿshā said: ‘She departed, having left in the heart, despite her distance, a crack that spread …’ meaning extended and pervasive.

His saying, ‘and they give food, despite their love for it, to the needy’: these righteous people give food despite loving and desiring it. Mujāhid said they themselves crave the food. Sulaymān ibn Qays, Abū Muqātil, explained it as their love of the food.

‘The needy’ means people whom need has humbled. ‘The orphan’ is a child whose father has died and who has no property. ‘The captive’ is a combatant from enemy territory captured by force and victory, or a member of the Muslim community detained lawfully. God praised these righteous people for feeding them, seeking nearness to God and His approval, and showing them mercy. Scholars differed about the captive meant here. Qatādah said God commanded kindness to captives, who at that time were polytheists. He added that a Muslim brother has an even greater right to be fed. ʿIkrimah likewise said the captives then were polytheists; al-Ḥasan said their captives were only polytheists.

Others said the verse means a prisoner from the Muslim community. Mujāhid said a captive is a prisoner. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said the needy, orphan, and captive may be from the Muslim community or others; ʿAṭāʾ agreed. Mujāhid also said the captive is one held in confinement. The sound view, al-Ṭabarī says, is that God describes the righteous as feeding captives generally. The name ‘captive’ can apply to both groups, and the report is general unless reliable evidence restricts it. Even if the captives at that time were only polytheists, the verse does not restrict those who fulfill vows to that period. It speaks about all people possessing this quality then and thereafter until the Resurrection, and includes both polytheist and Muslim captives.

His saying, ‘We feed you only for God’s sake’: when they feed these people, they say they do so seeking God’s approval and nearness to Him. ‘We desire from you neither recompense nor thanks’: they tell those they feed that they seek no reward or gratitude in return. ‘Thanks’ may be a plural of ‘thankfulness,’ like fulūs as the plural of fals and kufūr as the plural of kufr; or it may be a singular verbal noun used with a collective sense. Mujāhid said they did not actually say these words, but God knew this was in their hearts and praised them for it, so that others might aspire to do likewise. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr gave the same explanation.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘We fear from our Lord a grim, distressful Day (10), so God will protect them from the evil of that Day and grant them radiance and joy (11).’ God reports what these people say to the needy and others they feed: ‘We do not feed you to receive compensation for feeding you, nor thanks; rather, we feed you hoping that our Lord will keep us safe from His punishment on a Day whose terrors are severe …’ … when its faces will scowl from its hardships, and its people’s trial will be long and severe. Qamṭarīr describes something intense: one says ‘a qamṭarīr day,’ ‘a qumāṭir day,’ or ‘a ʿaṣīb / ʿaṣabṣab day.’ When a day becomes qamṭarīr, it is among the most severe and prolonged in hardship.
‘O sons of our uncle, do you remember our trial upon you, when a grim day came?’
The interpreters offered differing expressions of its meaning.

Some said a person will frown, furrowing the space between his eyes until sweat like tar runs down from between them. Ibn ʿAbbās said the disbeliever will frown so severely that sweat like tar runs between his eyes. Another report from him explains qamṭarīr as one who furrows the space between his eyes. Ibn ʿAbbās repeatedly explained qamṭarīr as furrowing the space between the eyes. He also described the Day as one on which a person will contract the space between his eyes and his face. Qatādah said faces will scowl and furrow their brows in aversion to that Day. He also said foreheads will be contracted, while some say qamṭarīr means severe. Mujāhid likewise explained it as the face contracting between the eyes.
Others said ʿabūs means constricted and qamṭarīr means long. Ibn ʿAbbās explained ʿabūs as constricted and qamṭarīr as long.
Others said qamṭarīr means severe. Ibn Zayd explained ʿabūs as evil and qamṭarīr as severe.

His saying, ‘So God will protect them from the evil of that Day and grant them radiance and joy’: God says … … He will shield them from the evil of the grim, distressful Day that they feared, because of the deeds they did in this world that pleased their Lord. He will grant radiance to their faces and joy to their hearts. Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah both explained it as radiance in the faces and joy in the hearts. Ibn Zayd said it means blessing and joy.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘He will reward them for their patience with a Garden and silk (12), reclining there upon couches; they will see neither sun nor bitter cold (13).’ God says that He will reward them with a Garden and silk for patiently obeying Him in this world and doing what pleases Him.
The interpreters said similarly. Qatādah explained the reward as a Garden and silk for their patience in obeying God and refraining from disobedience and what He had forbidden.

His saying, ‘reclining there upon couches’: they will recline in Paradise on beds in canopied chambers; these are the arāʾik, singular arīkah. This has already been explained with supporting evidence and the views of interpreters, so there is no need to repeat it all here. Ibn ʿAbbās said they are canopied chambers. Qatādah said they are canopied chambers containing beds. Mujāhid likewise said they are beds in canopied chambers. ‘Reclining’ is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier referring to the people rewarded: He rewarded them with a Garden while they recline in it.
His saying, ‘they will see neither sun nor bitter cold’: God means they will see neither a sun whose heat harms them … … nor bitter cold, which would harm them with its chill.

The interpreters said similarly. Mujāhid explained zamharīr as intense cold. Qatādah said God knows that extreme heat and extreme cold both cause harm, so He protected them from both. Murrah ibn ʿAbd Allāh said zamharīr is a kind of punishment, citing ‘They will taste neither coolness nor drink’ (Q 78:24). Abū Hurayrah related from the Prophet that Hell complained to its Lord, saying that its parts were consuming one another; God allowed it two breaths each year. The most severe cold people experience is from Hell’s zamharīr, and the most severe heat is from its heat.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘Its shade will draw near over them, and its clusters will be made to hang low in perfect ease (14); vessels of silver and cups that are crystal will be passed around among them (15).’ God means that the shade of the trees will be near them. There are several grammatical explanations for the accusative form of ‘drawing near’: it can be coordinated with ‘reclining’; coordinated with the syntactic position of ‘they will see no sun,’ since that too is accusative in meaning (‘reclining … and not seeing any sun’); or used as praise, as if saying ‘reclining … and, moreover, with its shade drawing near.’ In the last construction an understood verb governs it. It is feminine because ‘shades’ is a collective noun. In ʿAbd Allāh’s reading it is masculine, ‘drawing near over them are its shades,’ because the verb precedes its subject. Another reported reading has the nominative ‘drawing near,’ as a new sentence.
His saying, ‘and its clusters will be made to hang low’: the fruit of its trees will be made easy for them to pick however they wish, whether standing, sitting, or reclining.

The interpreters said similarly. Mujāhid said the branches rise to a person’s reach when he stands and lower to him when he sits or reclines, so he can take the fruit. Qatādah said no distance or thorns will keep their hands from it. Ibn Zayd explained ‘its fruit is near’ (Q 69:23) as meaning that the fruit has drawn close to them. Sufyān said they take it however they wish, sitting or reclining.

His saying, ‘vessels of silver and cups that are crystal’: vessels from which these righteous people drink will be passed around; they are made of silver yet are crystal-clear. Thus they combine the whiteness of silver with the clarity of glass.

The interpreters said similarly. Ibn ʿAbbās said they are vessels of silver whose clarity and finish resemble crystal. Mujāhid said they combine the delicacy of crystal with silver’s clarity. He also explained ‘crystal made of silver’ as crystal-clear yet made of silver. Qatādah said they have the clarity of crystal and the whiteness of silver.

His saying, ‘and cups’: large pitchers containing drink will be passed around with the vessels. Any large pitcher without a handle is called a kūb. Mujāhid said they have no handles. In another transmission of the same report and chain, Mujāhid said that the cups are drinking goblets.

His saying, ‘that were crystal’: these vessels and cups were crystal, then God transformed them into silver. It has also been said that describing the vessels passed around to the people of Paradise as silver indicates that Paradise’s soil is silver, since vessels are made from the earth’s soil. Readers differed in reciting ‘crystal’ and ‘chains.’ Most readers of Medina and Kufa, except Ḥamzah, read both with an alif and nunation, as they appear in their codices. Ḥamzah omits the alifs throughout and leaves the words uninflected. Abū ʿAmr retains the alif in the first occurrence of ‘crystal’ but not the second. Al-Ṭabarī considers all these readings sound, though Abū ʿAmr’s is preferable to him because the first occurrence ends a verse, and matching the other verse endings by retaining the alif in most of them is more pleasing.

x: The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘Crystal made of silver, measured precisely (16); they will be given a cup there whose mixture is ginger (17), from a spring there called Salsabīl (18).’ God says it is crystal at the height of crystal-like clarity and silver at the height of silver’s whiteness. Al-Ḥasan said ‘crystal made of silver’ means crystal’s clarity together with silver’s whiteness. He also described it as silver-white with the transparency of crystal. Abū Ṣāliḥ said its soil was silver.

It combines glass-like clarity with silver’s whiteness. Qatādah said that if people of falsehood tried to make a silver vessel through which one could see what lay behind it as clearly as through crystal, they would be unable to do so. He also said the vessels are silver with the clarity of crystal and the whiteness of silver. Mujāhid similarly described them as combining crystal’s clarity and silver’s whiteness.
His saying, ‘measured precisely’: they have measured those vessels passed around to them … … to match their need to quench their thirst, neither more nor less.

The interpreters said similarly. Al-Ḥasan said the vessels are measured according to the people’s thirst. Saʿīd likewise said they are sized to quench it. Mujāhid said they neither fall short nor overflow. In another report he said they are full: they do not spill, and their drink does not diminish. Qatādah said they are measured for their thirst. Qatādah said the cups are measured to quench the people’s thirst. Ibn Zayd said they are sized to the amount the people of Paradise drink. Mujāhid said they are full, do not spill, and are not deficient.

Others said the vessels are measured to fit the hand. Ibn ʿAbbās gave this explanation. Readers differed over ‘they measured them precisely’: most readers of the regions read the qāf with fatḥah, meaning that the cupbearers measure the vessels for them. It is reported that al-Shaʿbī and other early authorities read it with ḍammah, meaning that the cups are measured for them, with neither addition nor deficiency. The reading that I do not permit anyone to depart from is with fatḥah on the qāf, because the authoritative readers unanimously agree on it.

x: His saying, ‘they will be given a cup there whose mixture is ginger’: these righteous people will be given a cup in Paradise. A vessel is called a cup when it contains a drink; once empty, it is simply a vessel. Similarly, a tray carrying a gift is called a mihdā; once the gift is removed, it is a tray or serving platter, not a gift tray. The drink in the cup will be mixed with ginger.

The interpreters differed: some said their drink will be mixed with ginger. Qatādah said it is mixed with ginger. Mujāhid said they will be given the taste of what they used to drink in this world, and the report adds that it will be made beloved to them.

Others said Zanjabīl is the name of a spring from which the righteous people’s drink is mixed. Qatādah said it is a lofty spring: those brought near to God drink it unmixed, while it is mixed for the rest of the people of Paradise.

His saying, ‘from a spring there called Salsabīl’: a spring in Paradise called Salsabīl. It is said that the name means the water flows smoothly and readily. Qatādah said it is a spring whose water flows easily and is at their disposal. He also said they can direct its smooth-flowing water wherever they wish.

Others said it means that the spring runs swiftly. Mujāhid said the spring runs swiftly; he repeated this explanation in several reports, and also described it as flowing smoothly. Arab grammarians differed over the meaning and grammatical form of Salsabīl. Some Basran grammarians said it describes the spring’s smooth, continuous flow.

Others said the spring is called Salsabīl because of its pleasantness, just as certain famous camel breeds are named by their lineage. The Qur’an was revealed in the Arabs’ language. One grammarian recited a verse: ‘A yellow bow of nabʿ wood, its arrow called Sahm …’ and explained that the word after ‘called’ describes the noun rather than being the name itself. Another grammarian said the word is the proper name of the spring, made indefinite in form and given an alif at the verse ending like ‘crystal.’ A Kufan grammarian said it describes water that goes down the throat smoothly. Another reported that it is both a spring name and a description of water for its smoothness and sweetness. He argued that if it were a proper name, it would more usually be left uninflected, though Arabic can inflect words normally indeclinable in poetry; a verse by Mutammim ibn Nuwayrah does so with rawāʾim.

Al-Ṭabarī says the correct view is that ‘called Salsabīl’ describes the spring: it is smooth to the throat, flows easily, and submits to the people of Paradise, who direct it where they wish, as Mujāhid and Qatādah said. ‘Called’ means ‘described.’ This is preferable because the interpreters agree that Salsabīl functions as a description, not a proper name. The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘Immortal youths will circulate among them; when you see them, you would think them scattered pearls (19). When you look there, you will see bliss and a great kingdom (20).’ God says that youths—servants—will circulate among these righteous people.
The interpreters differed over ‘immortal.’
Some said it means they do not die. Qatādah explained it this way.
Others said they are adorned with bracelets; still others said they wear earrings. It was also said that they remain forever young and never change from that age.

In Arabic, an older man whose hair remains black may be called mukhallad; likewise, one whose teeth remain firmly in place. The word indicates permanence of condition. This supports Qatādah’s explanation: they do not die, since they remain unchanged by old age, gray hair, or death. It is also said that in the language of Ḥimyar mukhallad means ‘adorned with bracelets.’ One of their poets said: ‘Adorned with silver, as though their hindquarters were dunes …’ His saying, ‘when you see them, you would think them scattered pearls’: when you see these youths gathered or dispersed, Muḥammad, their beauty, the clear whiteness of their faces, and their multitude make them seem like scattered or heaped pearls. Qatādah said their appearance and beauty, and their numbers, make them like scattered pearls. Qatādah likewise said that their beauty and great number make them seem like scattered pearls. He related from Abū Ayyūb, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, that every inhabitant of Paradise will have a thousand youths serving him, each assigned a particular task. Sufyān explained ‘you would think them scattered pearls’ as referring to the multitude and whiteness of pearls.

His saying, ‘When you look there, you will see bliss’: God says to His Prophet Muḥammad: when you look with your eyes and cast your gaze upon the honors given to the righteous in Paradise. ‘There’ means Paradise. You will see bliss because even the lowest in rank, it is said, will look over his kingdom for a distance of two thousand years, seeing its farthest reaches as clearly as its nearest. Arab grammarians differed about why the object of the first ‘you see’ is omitted. Some Basrans said it is an intransitive seeing, as when one says, ‘I thought in the house,’ stating where the thought occurred; here he states where the seeing occurs. Some Kufans said the meaning is ‘when you see what is there, you will see bliss,’ with ‘what’ understood as in ‘your connection has been cut off’ (Q 6:94), meaning what was between you. It may also mean ‘when you look there’—when you cast your gaze in that direction, you will see bliss.

His saying, ‘and a great kingdom’: along with the bliss they see there, they will see a great dominion. It is said that this great kingdom consists in the angels greeting them and asking permission to enter. Mujāhid and Sufyān said it is the angels’ greeting; Sufyān also said they ask permission to enter.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘Upon them are garments of fine green silk and brocade; they will be adorned with bracelets of silver, and their Lord will give them a purifying drink (21).’ God says fine-silk garments will be above these righteous people. Some interpreters understood this as over the canopied chambers built over them. That view is not implausible: if the garments are above the chambers in which they sit, they are above the people as well. Readers differed in reciting ‘upon them’: most readers of Medina and Kufa and some of Mecca read it with a still yāʾ, as a word meaning ‘above them.’ ʿĀṣim, Abū ʿAmr, and Ibn Kathīr read the yāʾ with fatḥah, making it a noun governing ‘garments,’ like saying, ‘Their outer side is silk.’ Al-Ṭabarī says both are established readings with closely related meanings, and either is correct.

evidence.text: Readers differed in reciting ‘upon them’: most readers of Medina and Kufa and some of Mecca read it with a still yāʾ, as a word meaning ‘above them.’

x: His saying, ‘garments of sundus’: garments of fine, beautiful brocade. Sundus is the delicate, fine kind of brocade.

Readers differed in reciting ‘green’ and ‘brocade.’ Abū Jaʿfar and Abū ʿAmr read ‘green’ in the nominative as an adjective for the garments and ‘brocade’ in the genitive, coordinated with ‘sundus,’ meaning garments of brocade. ʿĀṣim and Ibn Kathīr read ‘green’ in the genitive and ‘brocade’ in the nominative, coordinating brocade with the garments and making ‘green’ an adjective of the sundus. Nāfiʿ read both ‘green’ and ‘brocade’ in the nominative, coordinating each with the garments. Most Kufan readers read both in the genitive. Ibn Muḥayṣin read ‘brocade’ without declension, with fatḥah, taking it to mean ‘garments of brocade’ and treating the word as foreign. Each of the readings mentioned has a grammatical basis, except the one attributed to Ibn Muḥayṣin, which is far from ordinary Arabic usage: istabraq is an indefinite noun, and Arabs inflect indefinite nouns even when they are foreign. Istabraq is thick brocade. The interpretations of the commentators have already been mentioned, so there is no need to repeat them. Qatādah said istabraq means thick brocade.

evidence.text: Most Kufan readers read both in the genitive.

x: His saying, ‘they will be adorned with bracelets of silver’: their Lord will adorn them with bracelets, plural of aswirah, made of silver.

His saying, ‘their Lord will give them a purifying drink’: He will give these righteous people a pure drink. Its purity includes that it does not become impure urine; instead, it becomes perspiration emerging from their bodies, fragrant like musk. Ibrāhīm al-Taymī said it is sweat flowing from their bodies like the scent of musk. Another report from him gives the same explanation. Ibrāhīm al-Taymī also said that a man among the people of Paradise will be granted the appetite, eating, and vigor of a hundred men of this world. When he eats, he is given a purifying drink; it becomes perspiration from his skin, more fragrant than the finest musk, and then his appetite returns. Mujāhid explained ‘purifying drink’ as the drinks mentioned. Abū Qilābah said that when the people of Paradise have eaten and drunk as they wish, they call for the purifying drink and drink it; it cleanses their stomachs, and what they ate and drank becomes perspiration with the fragrance of musk, so their stomachs become slender.

Abū Hurayrah—or someone else, as the transmitter Abū Jaʿfar al-Rāzī was uncertain—related that Gabriel took the Prophet up to the seventh heaven on the night of the Ascension. After the gate was opened, he entered and saw an elderly, gray-haired man seated on a chair at Paradise’s gate.

Some people beside him had faces white as sheets, while others had some discoloration. Those with discoloration entered one river and bathed; some of the discoloration disappeared. They entered a second river and bathed, and their color became clear, like that of their companions. The Prophet asked Gabriel who the gray-haired man, the white-faced people, and those with discoloration were, and what the rivers were. Gabriel said: ‘This is your father Abraham, the first person on earth to grow gray hair. Those with white faces are people who did not mingle their faith with wrongdoing. Those whose complexion was discolored are people who mixed good deeds with bad, then repented, and God accepted their repentance. The rivers are, in order, mercy, blessing, and the purifying drink their Lord gave them.’

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘This is your recompense, and your striving has been appreciated (22). We have sent down the Qur’an to you in stages (23), so be patient with your Lord’s judgment and do not obey any sinner or ingrate among them (24).’ God says that the righteous will be told: this honor We have given you is a reward for the good deeds you used to perform in this world. ‘Your striving has been appreciated’ means your deeds here have been praised: your Lord approved of them and rewarded you with this honor. Qatādah said God forgave them their sins and appreciated their good deeds. Qatādah explained ‘your striving has been appreciated’ as: God has appreciated even a small effort.

His saying, ‘We have sent down the Qur’an to you in stages’: God says to His Prophet Muḥammad that He sent the Qur’an down to him as a trial and test. ‘So be patient with your Lord’s judgment’: be patient with the obligations by which your Lord tests you, conveying His messages, and carrying out what He has required of you in the revelation sent to you. ‘Do not obey any sinner or ingrate among them’: do not obey any of the polytheists among your people in disobeying God. ‘Sinner’ means one who commits His prohibitions; ‘ingrate’ means one who denies His blessings and favors, disbelieves in Him, and worships another. It is said that Abū Jahl is meant. Qatādah said the verse was revealed concerning God’s enemy Abū Jahl. He also transmitted that Abū Jahl said, ‘If I see Muḥammad praying, I will step on his neck,’ after which God revealed ‘Do not obey any sinner or ingrate among them.’ Ibn Zayd said ‘sinner’ means a sinful wrongdoer, and ‘ingrate’ amounts to the same thing.

The phrase may mean ‘nor an ingrate.’ Al-Farrāʾ said ‘or’ here can function like ‘nor’ in a negative, question, or conditional sentence, as it does here in a negative context. He cited a poem: ‘No grief of a bereaved mother is like mine, nor the grief of a young camel that has lost its calf, or the grief of an old man who lost his she-camel when the pilgrims gathered and departed.’ The poet means ‘nor the grief of an old man.’ Arabic may also use ‘or’ with a meaning close to ‘and’: ‘I will certainly give you what you ask, or remain silent’ means that I will give it to you in any case.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘Remember the name of your Lord morning and evening (25), and during the night prostrate to Him and glorify Him through much of the night (26). These people love the immediate life and leave behind them a weighty Day (27).’ God says: Muḥammad, remember your Lord’s name and call upon Him in the morning in the dawn prayer and in the evening in the noon and afternoon prayers. ‘During the night, prostrate to Him’ means prostrate to Him in your night prayer. ‘Glorify Him through much of the night’ means for a large part of the night, as in ‘Stand in prayer at night, except for a little: half of it, or a little less, or a little more’ (Q 73:2–4).

The interpreters said similarly. Ibn ʿAbbās explained prostration and glorification during the night as prayer and glorification. Ibn Zayd said ‘morning’ means the dawn prayer and ‘evening’ the noon prayer.

He said this was the first thing made obligatory. He recited ‘O you who are wrapped up, stand through the night except a little, half of it’ (Q 73:1–3), and then ‘Your Lord knows that you stand for nearly two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it,’ through ‘so recite whatever is easy of the Qur’an’ (Q 73:20). He said this obligation was then lifted from the Messenger of God and the people, and made voluntary, as in ‘During the night, keep vigil with it as an extra devotion for you’ (Q 17:79). Thus it became voluntary.

His saying, ‘These people love the immediate life’: God means that these polytheists love this world, wish to remain in it, and are enamored of its adornments. ‘They leave behind them a weighty Day’ means that they abandon the deeds of the Hereafter and what would save them from God’s punishment on that Day … … Some interpreted the phrase to mean that they leave the weighty Day behind, which is not an impossible interpretation, though the meaning given above fits the wording better.
The interpreters said similarly. Sufyān explained ‘they leave behind them a weighty Day’ as the Hereafter.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘We created them and strengthened their constitution; and when We will, We can replace them with others like them completely (28). This is a reminder, so whoever wishes may take a way to his Lord (29).’ God says: We created these people who associate others with God and oppose His commands and prohibitions. ‘We strengthened their constitution’ means that We made their creation firm. In Arabic, one says a man was well constructed when he was created with a sound, well-formed constitution.
The interpreters said similarly. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as ‘We made their creation firm.’ Mujāhid …
… also explained ‘We strengthened their constitution’ as their physical creation. Qatādah gave the same explanation.
Others said asr means the joints. Ibn Zayd related from Abū Saʿīd, who had learned the Qur’an from Abū Hurayrah, that the word means the joints.

Others said it means strength; Ibn Zayd transmitted this view as well. Al-Ṭabarī says the most correct interpretation is the one he chose: among the Arabs, asr means the constitution or bodily structure, as in al-Akhṭal’s verse: ‘From every strong-built, well-bred horse, easy to guide, you might think him proud.’ People also say ‘take it in its entirety,’ meaning take all of it.

His saying, ‘when We will, We can replace them with others like them completely’: if We will, We will destroy these people and bring others of their kind in their place, similar in creation but different in their deeds.
The interpreters said similarly. Ibn Zayd said it means the children of Adam who disobeyed God, and others like them among Adam’s descendants.
His saying, ‘This is a reminder’: this sūrah is a reminder for whoever takes heed, accepts admonition, and reflects.
The interpreters said similarly. Qatādah said this sūrah is a reminder.
His saying, ‘whoever wishes may take a way to his Lord’: whoever among you wishes may take a path to his Lord’s approval by obeying Him and complying with His commands and prohibitions.

The interpretation of God’s saying: ‘You do not will unless God wills. God is indeed Knowing and Wise (30). He admits whom He wills into His mercy; and for the wrongdoers He has prepared a painful punishment (31).’ God says: people, you cannot will to take a path to your Lord unless God wills that for you, since the decision belongs to Him, not to you. In the reported reading of ʿAbd Allāh, it says: ‘You do not will except what God wills.’

evidence.text: In the reported reading of ʿAbd Allāh, it says: ‘You do not will except what God wills.’

x: His saying, ‘God is indeed Knowing and Wise’: none of you will escape what His prior knowledge has determined in His governance of you.

His saying, ‘He admits whom He wills into His mercy’: your Lord admits whichever of you He wills into His mercy, granting him repentance from his error until he dies repentant, forgiving his sins, and admitting him to His Garden. ‘For the wrongdoers He has prepared a painful punishment’ means those who wronged themselves and died associating others with God. He has prepared a painful and agonizing punishment for them in the Hereafter: the punishment of Hell. ‘And the wrongdoers’ is in the accusative because the conjunction w occupies the position of a preposition attached to ‘He prepared’; the sense is ‘and He prepared a painful punishment for the wrongdoers.’ It is reported that ʿAbd Allāh’s reading says ‘and for the wrongdoers He prepared for them,’ repeating the preposition, a construction Arabs sometimes use.
‘I say to her, when she asks for divorce: why are you hastening to leave me?’
‘Then they no longer ask him what is wrong with him: has he risen in the valley of passion, or descended?’
The bāʾ is repeated; the intended wording is ‘they do not ask him about what is wrong with him.’ This is the end of the commentary on Sūrat al-Insān.
